strengths: Clear and well-motivated analysis of temperature effects on representation learning (Section 3), explaining the trade-off between instance-level and semantic-level features with intuitive examples

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (CIFAR, TinyImageNet, semantic shift benchmarks), loss functions (CE, SupCon, ARPL), and metrics (accuracy, AUROC, OSCR) with proper ablation studies

Practical utility with zero computational overhead—the method integrates seamlessly into any temperature-dependent loss function, unlike prior OSR methods requiring auxiliary models or data augmentation
Strong improvements on harder semantic shift benchmarks with increasing number of training classes (Figure 3), showing the method addresses the tougher OSR scenarios
Excellent reproducibility: detailed training details, standard deviations across 5 seeds, implementation code provided, and promise of code release
weaknesses: Limited novelty: temperature scaling and scheduling are well-established; the core contribution is reversing an existing cosine schedule (k=0 → k=1), making this feel incremental for a top-tier venue

Modest and inconsistent improvements: many gains are 1-2% within standard deviation ranges; clear failures exist (e.g., Aircraft SupCon+LS shows degradation; minimal CIFAR improvements); success seems context-dependent

Weak theoretical justification: the explanation that 'unknown samples stay distributed because features are unknown' is circular; why low-then-high temperature specifically helps OSR versus other scheduling patterns lacks rigor

Experimental setup concerns: paper uses different pretrained model for semantic shift benchmarks than prior work (Vaze et al. 2022, footnote 1), undermining direct comparison; baseline constant temperatures not thoroughly tuned

strengths: Clear motivation with intuitive visualization (Figure 1) showing the temperature trade-off between instance-level and semantic-level features
Practical approach with zero computational overhead, seamlessly integrable into any loss function (CE, SupCon, ARPL)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (SSBs, TinyImageNet, CIFAR), loss functions, and ablations on hyperparameters (P, k, τ+ and τ-)
Consistent (though modest) improvements across most tested configurations with standard deviations reported across 5 random seeds
Sound mathematical analysis (Section 3) with gradient derivations explaining how temperature controls hard negative mining vs semantic clustering
Well-documented supplementary materials including implementation code, training details, and results with vision transformers
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Temperature scheduling was already proposed by Kukleva et al. (2023); this work mainly reverses the schedule direction (k=1 phase shift). Even simple linear schedules (Table 1) achieve nearly equivalent performance (Linear: 4 wins vs P-NegCosSch: 8 wins out of 18 metrics), questioning the necessity of the proposed cosine form

Modest empirical improvements that often fall within noise margins: typical gains of 1-2% AUROC on SSBs; minimal improvements on CIFAR benchmarks (Table 9: ~0.06% AUROC); some cases show degradation (e.g., Aircraft SupCon+LS: -1.4% AUROC). Standard deviations (Tables 3-4) suggest many improvements are within 1-2 standard deviations

Weak justification for NegCosSch specifically: If linear/exponential schedules work nearly as well, why introduce mathematical complexity (Eq. 5-7) for the generalized cosine schedule? The paper doesn't convincingly argue for the necessity of the cosine form over simpler alternatives

Ad-hoc hyperparameter selection strategy: Proposed method for choosing (τ+, τ-) requires knowing a good constant temperature already; CE loss uses different relationship (τ+ = 2τ, τ- = τ/2) without clear justification; limited analysis of sensitivity to these choices

Limited generalizability: Minimal or negligible improvements on CIFAR benchmarks, attributed to fewer training classes (Appendix F.6), undermining claims of broad applicability beyond SSBs with many classes

Incomplete theoretical foundation: 'Familiarity Hypothesis' is cited but not deeply integrated; connection between alternating instance-level/semantic-level learning and OSR improvement could be formalized more rigorously; no clear differentiation from curriculum learning

Missing robustness analysis: No discussion of failure cases (e.g., Aircraft SupCon+LS negative improvement); limited guidance on when constant temperature is preferable; UMAP visualizations (Figure 1) lack supporting quantitative cluster metrics (silhouette score, Davies-Bouldin index)

Ablation shows schedule form is not critical: Period P ablation (Table 6) shows varying P produces similar performance, suggesting the specific functional form is less important than simply varying temperature gradually

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (regular OSR + semantic shift benchmarks), loss functions (CE, SupCon, ARPL), architectures (VGG, ResNet, ViT), and with thorough ablations. Results averaged over 5 random seeds with standard deviations reported.

Excellent clarity of motivation and intuition. Figure 1's UMAP visualizations effectively demonstrate the temperature-feature trade-off and how the proposed schedule addresses it. The gradient analysis clearly connects temperature scaling to representation learning properties.

Exceptional practicality: trivial to implement (few lines of code, Appendix H), zero computational overhead, applicable to any temperature-dependent loss function without modification. Easy adoption path for practitioners.

Meaningful focus on harder semantic shift benchmarks with 'Easy' and 'Hard' splits rather than only standard benchmarks. Recognition that smaller regular benchmarks are insufficient for realistic evaluation.
Insightful analysis showing benefits scale with number of training classes (Section 5.3), providing understanding of when the method is most beneficial and how it performs as problems become harder.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: temperature scheduling already exists in prior work (Kukleva et al., 2023). The main contribution is reversing schedule direction and applying to OSR—a relatively straightforward adaptation that feels incremental.

Improvements are modest and inconsistent: typically 1-3% on AUROC/OSCR, with many improvements within reported standard deviations. On CIFAR benchmarks (Table 9) improvements are negligible (<0.5%). Some cases show degradation (e.g., TinyImageNet CE+LS: 84.55%→84.24%). No formal significance testing performed.

Theoretical justification is shallow. The paper provides intuition for why low-then-high temperature helps, but lacks rigorous analysis of: (1) why this direction is better than alternatives, (2) convergence properties, or (3) generalization bounds. The reversal of CosSch is asserted to work but not rigorously explained.

Hyperparameter tuning still required despite simplicity claims: must choose τ⁺ and τ⁻, guided only by ad-hoc heuristics (Δ≈0.1-0.2 for SupCon; τ⁺=2τ, τ⁻=τ/2 for CE). Figure 4 ablation shows sensitivity to these choices, implying tuning cost is non-negligible.

Performance highly dataset-dependent with inconsistent benefits: negligible improvements on CIFAR (only 4-6 training classes), outright degradation in some cases (Aircraft+SupCon+LS, TinyImageNet+CE+LS in Table 2). Raises questions about when method is applicable.

Multiple TS variants (P-NegCosSch, M-NegCosSch, linear, exponential) complicate guidance to practitioners. Differences often small, and formulation (Eq. 5) with kπ shift parameter is convoluted. Unclear which variant to recommend.

Limited analysis of when/why method fails or succeeds. Label smoothing interaction unexplained (sometimes helps, sometimes hurts). CosSch vs NegCosSch differences often small. Missing investigation of: learnable temperature, why CIFAR fails, or deeper failure mode analysis.
